title: The OWASP essentials
intro: Security problems often come from ordinary application features rather than exotic attacks. This lesson introduces the OWASP risks you are most likely to encounter as a junior full-stack developer and shows the practical habits that prevent them.
body:
## What is OWASP? **OWASP**, the Open Worldwide Application Security Project, is a community focused on improving software security. One of its best-known resources is the **OWASP Top 10**, a living list of major categories of web application security risks. You do not need to memorize the list to write safer software. What matters is learning to recognize common failure patterns and knowing what to do instead. As a full-stack developer, you will encounter security decisions in controllers, database queries, React components, configuration files, dependencies, logs, and deployment settings. The examples in this lesson use the task manager because security becomes easier to understand when you connect it to features you are actually building. ## Broken access control **Broken access control** happens when an application fails to enforce who is allowed to access or modify a resource. ~~~compare {"left": {"title": "Trusting the id", "lang": "java", "code": "@GetMapping(\"/api/orders/{id}\")\nOrder get(@PathVariable long id) {\n return repo.findById(id).orElseThrow();\n}", "note": "Change 41 to 42 in the URL and read someone else's order (IDOR)."}, "right": {"title": "Checking ownership", "lang": "java", "code": "Order get(long id, User me) {\n return repo.findByIdAndOwner(id, me)\n .orElseThrow(NotFound::new);\n}", "note": "Scope every query to the current user."}} ~~~ A classic example is **IDOR**, or Insecure Direct Object Reference. Imagine the task API has: ~~~text GET /api/tasks/123 ~~~ A user is allowed to access task `123`, so everything appears fine. But what happens if they change the URL to: ~~~text GET /api/tasks/124 ~~~ If task `124` belongs to another user and the backend returns it anyway, you have an authorization vulnerability. ### Bad example ~~~java @GetMapping("/api/tasks/{id}") public Task getTask(@PathVariable Long id) { return taskRepository.findById(id).orElseThrow(); } ~~~ This code checks whether the task exists, but not whether the authenticated user is allowed to see it. ### Good example The backend should include authorization in the operation: ~~~java @GetMapping("/api/tasks/{id}") public Task getTask( @PathVariable Long id, Authentication authentication) { return taskService.getTaskForUser(id, authentication.getName()); } ~~~ The service can then verify ownership or another access rule before returning the task. The important lesson is that **knowing an object's ID does not grant permission to access it**. ## Injection **Injection** happens when untrusted data changes the meaning of a command or query. ~~~compare {"left": {"title": "String concatenation", "lang": "java", "code": "\"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '\"\n + email + \"'\"\n// email = \"' OR '1'='1\"", "note": "Input becomes part of the SQL — attacker controls the query."}, "right": {"title": "Parameters", "lang": "java", "code": "@Query(\"select u from User u where u.email = :email\")\nOptional find(@Param(\"email\") String email);", "note": "The value is sent separately and never parsed as SQL."}} ~~~ SQL injection is a classic example. Imagine building SQL by concatenating user input. ### Bad example ~~~java String sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'"; ~~~ If `email` contains specially crafted SQL, the resulting query can have a different meaning from what the developer intended. ### Good example Use parameterized queries so data remains data: ~~~java @Query("SELECT u FROM UserEntity u WHERE u.email = :email") Optional findByEmail(@Param("email") String email); ~~~ JPA and Spring Data provide mechanisms for binding parameters rather than concatenating them into queries. Prepared statements provide the same fundamental protection for lower-level JDBC code. The rule is simple: **never construct SQL by concatenating untrusted input**. Injection is not limited to SQL. Similar problems can occur when untrusted data becomes part of shell commands, LDAP queries, template expressions, or other interpretable input. ## Cross-site scripting **XSS**, or Cross-Site Scripting, happens when an attacker manages to make a victim's browser execute malicious content as part of your website. Imagine a comment feature where someone submits: ~~~html ~~~ ### Bad example A developer might inject the comment directly into HTML: ~~~js comments.innerHTML += `
  • ${comment}
    • `; ~~~ The browser interprets the input as HTML instead of treating it as ordinary text. ### Good example Create elements and assign user input with `textContent`: ~~~js const li = document.createElement("li"); li.textContent = comment; comments.appendChild(li); ~~~ React normally escapes values rendered in JSX: ~~~tsx

    {comment}

    ~~~ The comment is treated as text rather than interpreted as HTML. Be especially careful with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. The name is intentionally a warning. If you use it with untrusted input, you can introduce XSS. If an application genuinely needs to render user-provided HTML, it needs a carefully designed sanitization strategy rather than simply trusting the input. ## Cross-site request forgery **CSRF**, or Cross-Site Request Forgery, tricks a user's browser into making an authenticated request they did not intend to make. This matters especially when authentication credentials are automatically attached to requests, such as browser cookies. For example, imagine a banking application authenticates entirely with a session cookie. A malicious website could attempt to cause the victim's browser to submit a request to the bank while the bank's cookie is automatically included. ### Bad example ~~~text Browser automatically sends session cookie ↓ Malicious page causes POST request ↓ Server trusts cookie without CSRF protection ~~~ ### Good example Use appropriate CSRF protection for cookie-based authentication. Depending on the architecture, this can involve CSRF tokens and carefully configured cookie policies such as `SameSite`. For a stateless API that authenticates requests using an `Authorization: Bearer` header rather than automatically attached cookies, the CSRF threat is different. That is why you should not blindly enable or disable CSRF protection without understanding how authentication credentials reach the server. ## Security misconfiguration Security vulnerabilities are not always caused by complicated code. Configuration mistakes are extremely common. Examples include: - Default usernames and passwords left enabled. - Debug mode enabled in production. - Detailed stack traces returned to users. - Unnecessary API endpoints exposed publicly. - Overly broad CORS configuration. - Unnecessary services and ports exposed to the internet. **CORS**, or Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, controls which browser origins are allowed to make certain cross-origin requests. ### Bad example ~~~java configuration.setAllowedOrigins(List.of("*")); ~~~ A wildcard can be appropriate for genuinely public resources, but using unrestricted CORS for a private authenticated application without understanding the consequences is dangerous. ### Good example Allow only the origins your application actually needs: ~~~text https://softwaredevelopment.hu https://app.example.com ~~~ Similarly, never deploy with default administrator passwords. Production configuration should explicitly define appropriate credentials, permissions, network exposure, and error handling. ## Sensitive data exposure Sensitive information can leak in places developers do not expect. Consider a login failure where the application logs the complete request: ### Bad example ~~~java log.info("Login request: {}", request); ~~~ If the request contains a password, the password may now exist in log files, monitoring systems, backups, or third-party log services. Other common mistakes include: - Committing API keys or JWT secrets to Git. - Logging passwords or access tokens. - Sending sensitive data over plain HTTP. - Returning unnecessary personal data from APIs. - Including secrets in frontend JavaScript. ### Good example Log useful diagnostic information without credentials: ~~~java log.info("Login attempt for user {}", email); ~~~ Use HTTPS in production so traffic is encrypted in transit. Keep secrets in secure configuration rather than source code, and expose only the data an API consumer actually needs. Remember that anything shipped to the browser should be considered visible to the user. A secret embedded in React's production JavaScript is not a secret. ## Vulnerable dependencies Modern applications depend on many libraries. Your project might directly depend on Spring Boot, React, PostgreSQL drivers, and dozens of transitive dependencies. A **transitive dependency** is a library that your application receives indirectly because another dependency requires it. A vulnerability in one of those packages can affect your application even if you never directly imported the vulnerable code. ### Bad example ~~~text Install dependency once ↓ Never update or inspect it ↓ Known vulnerability remains in production ~~~ ### Good example Keep dependencies maintained and use automated checks where possible. GitHub's Dependabot can identify dependency updates and known vulnerabilities. For Maven projects, tools such as `mvn dependency:check` can help identify known vulnerable dependencies. For JavaScript projects, `npm audit` can report known vulnerabilities in installed packages. These tools are not a guarantee that your application is secure, but they are useful parts of a broader dependency-management process. ## Rate limiting login attempts Authentication endpoints are attractive targets for automated password guessing. If an attacker can send unlimited login requests, they can try large numbers of passwords against an account. ### Bad example ~~~text POST /api/auth/login POST /api/auth/login POST /api/auth/login ... unlimited attempts ... ~~~ ### Good example Apply **rate limiting**, which restricts how frequently requests can be made. For example, an application might limit repeated failed login attempts by IP address, account, or another appropriate identifier. The exact policy depends on your infrastructure and threat model. You can also combine rate limiting with MFA, strong password policies, account monitoring, and carefully designed authentication responses. Rate limiting is not only about security. It can also protect your application from accidental or intentional excessive traffic. ## Security headers and browser protections Modern browsers provide security mechanisms that applications can use through HTTP response headers. For example, a Content Security Policy, commonly called **CSP**, can restrict which scripts and other resources a browser is allowed to load. Spring Security can help configure security-related HTTP headers, but you should understand what each header is intended to protect rather than copying a configuration without understanding it. Security headers are another layer of defence. They do not replace correct authorization, safe database access, output handling, or secure authentication. ## A practical security mindset Security is easier when you treat every boundary as something that needs validation. Ask questions such as: ~~~text Who supplied this value? Can the user change it? What happens if it contains unexpected characters? Who is allowed to access this resource? Could this information end up in logs? What happens if this dependency is compromised? What happens when authentication expires? ~~~ For the task manager, that means checking the authenticated user before returning a task, using parameterized database queries, rendering comments as text, protecting authentication endpoints from abuse, and keeping secrets outside source code. ## Common mistakes ### “The frontend already checks it” Frontend checks improve UX but cannot enforce security. Always repeat authorization decisions on the backend. ### Concatenating SQL Never build SQL by joining strings containing untrusted input. Use parameters, prepared statements, JPA, or Spring Data query parameters. ### Using innerHTML for convenience Direct HTML injection can turn user input into executable markup. Prefer `textContent` or normal React JSX rendering for untrusted text. ### Logging everything Logs are useful, but they can become a second database of sensitive information. Never casually log passwords, tokens, secrets, or complete sensitive request objects. ### Allowing every origin CORS should match your application's actual cross-origin requirements. A permissive configuration is not automatically harmless. ### Ignoring dependencies A project can be vulnerable because of a transitive dependency you never knowingly installed. Keep dependencies monitored and updated. ## Security is layered No single technique protects a modern application. ~~~diagram {"type": "layers", "title": "Defence in depth", "caption": "No single layer is perfect; together they make attacks expensive.", "layers": [{"label": "Browser", "items": ["CSP", "HttpOnly cookies", "escaping in React"]}, {"label": "Edge", "items": ["HTTPS", "rate limiting", "WAF"]}, {"label": "API", "items": ["authentication", "authorization", "validation"], "highlight": true}, {"label": "Data", "items": ["parameterised SQL", "least privilege DB user", "backups"]}, {"label": "Supply chain", "items": ["Dependabot", "npm audit", "OWASP dependency-check"]}]} ~~~ A secure task manager combines multiple layers: ~~~text Authentication ↓ Authorization ↓ Input handling ↓ Safe database access ↓ Output encoding ↓ Secure configuration ↓ Dependency management ↓ Monitoring and rate limiting ↓ Secure deployment ~~~ If one layer fails, another layer can reduce the impact. For example, suppose an attacker finds a way to execute JavaScript through an XSS vulnerability. Strong cookie configuration can make credential theft harder. Backend authorization can still prevent the attacker from accessing another user's task. Rate limiting can reduce some automated abuse. Good logging can help you detect suspicious behaviour. This is why security is not a single feature you add at the end of development. It is a collection of decisions made throughout the application. The OWASP Top 10 is useful as a starting point and a shared vocabulary, but it is not a complete security checklist. Keep learning, keep dependencies updated, and treat security requirements as part of normal application development.
takeaways: Broken access control is especially dangerous in APIs because knowing a resource ID must never imply permission to access it.
Use parameterized database access and safe output rendering instead of trusting or concatenating user input.
Protect secrets, cookies, configuration, dependencies, and authentication endpoints as carefully as your application code.
Frontend validation improves UX, but backend authorization and validation must remain the security boundary.
The OWASP Top 10 is a living list that provides useful categories for understanding common application security risks.

quiz.question: What is the core problem in an IDOR vulnerability such as an insecure /api/tasks/{id} endpoint?
options: The task ID is too long
The frontend uses React
The server fails to verify whether the current user is allowed to access the referenced task
The database uses PostgreSQL
quiz.explanation: IDOR is a broken access-control problem. The server must verify that the authenticated user is authorized to access the specific resource identified by the request.

quiz.question: Which approach is safer for a user-provided email in a database query?
options: Concatenate the email directly into an SQL string
Use a parameterized query or JPA/Spring Data parameter
Remove all spaces from the email and concatenate it
Base64-encode the email before concatenating it
quiz.explanation: Parameterized queries keep user input separate from the query structure, preventing the input from changing the intended SQL command.

quiz.question:
Why is React JSX such as

{comment}

generally safer than inserting the comment with innerHTML?
options: React normally escapes the value instead of interpreting it as HTML
React automatically encrypts every comment
JSX removes all special characters from the user's input
innerHTML cannot render text
quiz.explanation: React normally escapes values rendered through JSX, so user input is treated as text rather than interpreted as HTML. Direct HTML injection requires much more care.

quiz.question: When is CSRF particularly relevant?
options: When a browser automatically sends authentication credentials such as cookies
Only when PostgreSQL is installed on Linux
Only when a React component has more than 100 lines
Whenever a password contains a number
quiz.explanation: CSRF is especially relevant when authentication credentials are automatically attached to browser requests, such as session cookies. Bearer headers have a different request model.

quiz.question: Which is an example of sensitive data exposure?
options: Using TypeScript interfaces
Creating a React component for a task list
Logging an authentication request that contains a user's password
Using a parameterized JPA query
quiz.explanation: Passwords should not appear in logs because logs may be stored, copied, backed up, or accessed by other systems and people.

exercise.title: Render comments safely
exercise.task:
Build a safe comment renderer for a small comment page. The page already contains a form with id `comment-form`, an input with id `author`, a textarea with id `text`, a submit button, and an empty `
    ` with id `comments`. Write the script so that submitting the form adds one `
  • ` per valid comment. Each `
  • ` must contain a `` containing the trimmed author and a `` containing the trimmed comment text. Use `textContent` only for user-provided values; never use `innerHTML` to insert them. Ignore comments whose trimmed text is empty. Trim both author and text before rendering. Limit the text to 280 characters by cutting longer input to 280 characters. Clear the textarea after every submission, including when the submitted text is empty. Also implement `escapeHtml(str)`, replacing `&`, `<`, `>`, `"`, and `'` with `&`, `<`, `>`, `"`, and `'`. The tests submit malicious input such as `` and verify that no `img` element is created while the visible text remains exactly the typed text. The HTML structure and IDs are part of the exercise contract.
exercise.hint: Create the elements with `document.createElement`, then put the author and text into them with `textContent`. Do not build the comment HTML as a string. For `escapeHtml`, use a replacement map for the five characters and a regular expression that finds every occurrence.

tests.name: It renders a normal comment
tests.code: const author = document.getElementById("author"); const text = document.getElementById("text"); await typeInto(author, "Anna"); await typeInto(text, "Hello task manager!"); await click(document.querySelector("button")); const li = document.querySelector("#comments li"); if (!li) throw new Error("Comment was not added"); const strong = li.querySelector("strong"); const span = li.querySelector("span"); return strong && span && strong.textContent === "Anna" && span.textContent === "Hello task manager!";

tests.name: It renders malicious text as plain text
tests.code: const author = document.getElementById("author"); const text = document.getElementById("text"); const malicious = ""; await typeInto(author, "Attacker"); await typeInto(text, malicious); await click(document.querySelector("button")); const comments = document.getElementById("comments"); const img = comments.querySelector("img"); const span = comments.querySelector("span"); return !img && span && span.textContent === malicious;

tests.name: It trims the author and text
tests.code: await typeInto(document.getElementById("author"), "  Anna  "); await typeInto(document.getElementById("text"), "  Hello!  "); await click(document.querySelector("button")); const li = document.querySelector("#comments li"); return li.querySelector("strong").textContent === "Anna" && li.querySelector("span").textContent === "Hello!";

tests.name: It ignores an empty comment
tests.code: await typeInto(document.getElementById("author"), "Anna"); await typeInto(document.getElementById("text"), "   "); await click(document.querySelector("button")); return document.querySelectorAll("#comments li").length === 0;

tests.name: It limits comments to 280 characters
tests.code: const longText = "x".repeat(300); await typeInto(document.getElementById("author"), "Anna"); await typeInto(document.getElementById("text"), longText); await click(document.querySelector("button")); const span = document.querySelector("#comments li span"); return span && span.textContent.length === 280 && span.textContent === "x".repeat(280);

tests.name: It clears the textarea after submitting
tests.code: const text = document.getElementById("text"); await typeInto(document.getElementById("author"), "Anna"); await typeInto(text, "Hello"); await click(document.querySelector("button")); return text.value === "";

tests.name: It clears the textarea after an empty submission
tests.code: const text = document.getElementById("text"); await typeInto(document.getElementById("author"), "Anna"); await typeInto(text, "   "); await click(document.querySelector("button")); return text.value === "" && document.querySelectorAll("#comments li").length === 0;

tests.name: It escapes HTML characters
tests.code: const input = "& < > \" '"; const expected = "& < > " '"; return escapeHtml(input) === expected;

tests.name: It escapes every occurrence
tests.code: const input = "<<&>>\"''&"; const expected = "<<&>>"''&"; return escapeHtml(input) === expected;
